# Conclusion

This study contributes to the agricultural productivity literature by examining how disparities in farmland ownership influence access to technology and crop production efficiency among farmers in Ghana. While previous studies have explored various socioeconomic factors affecting agricultural productivity, the role of land tenure arrangements, and particularly the distinctions among ownership documentation, rights, and acquisition modes, remains underexplored. Using nationally representative farm-level data from the GLSS rounds 3-7 covering `r fmt_num(N_ALL, 0)` farm households, the study employs a MSF approach combined with matching techniques to assess disparities in technological endowment and efficiency linked to farmland ownership. The findings reveal that landowners and non-landowners exhibit comparable levels of technical efficiency, with aggregate differences below one percentage point. This indicates that under similar observable conditions, both groups convert inputs into outputs with similar effectiveness.

The study nonetheless uncovers meaningful heterogeneity across specific tenure arrangements. Relative to matched non-owners, documented owners and holders of transferable or collateral rights record meta-frontier efficiency shortfalls of roughly `r fmt_num(100*min(abs(c(tbl_num("table4.csv","Owned with documentation","c3"), tbl_num("table4.csv","Can be used as collateral security","c3"), tbl_num("table4.csv","Can be sold","c3"), tbl_num("table4.csv","Can be used as collateral security and sold","c3")))), 0)` to `r fmt_num(100*max(abs(c(tbl_num("table4.csv","Owned with documentation","c3"), tbl_num("table4.csv","Can be used as collateral security","c3"), tbl_num("table4.csv","Can be sold","c3"), tbl_num("table4.csv","Can be used as collateral security and sold","c3")))), 0)` percentage points. Within modes of land access, technical efficiency among farmers without ownership sits `r fmt_num(100*abs(max(unlist(lapply(objs$acq[c("rented","purchased","kinship")], function(x) x$te)))), 0)` to `r fmt_num(100*abs(min(unlist(lapply(objs$acq[c("rented","purchased","kinship")], function(x) x$te)))), 0)` percentage points below that of owners on rented, purchased, and family-allocated land, while on land accessed free of charge they perform at least as well as owners. No single tenure form therefore delivers a uniform advantage. Where ownership does carry an efficiency premium it is largest on purchased and rented land; where non-owners instead sit closer to the meta-frontier technology, that advantage is widest on purchased and sharecropped land.

Taken together, these results indicate that improving access to land alone is insufficient, but they also decline to support the simpler proposition that stronger formal tenure delivers better performance. Neither documentation nor an enforceable right to sell or pledge the land is associated with an overall performance premium relative to matched non-owners; on meta-frontier efficiency both run in the opposite direction. What does track ownership is the route by which land is obtained: on rented, purchased, and family-allocated land, owners convert inputs more efficiently than comparable non-owners, even as those non-owners sit closer to the best available technology. Tenure arrangements therefore matter for farm performance, but not in the direction that titling-centred prescriptions assume, and the sign of the ownership gap depends on which dimension of tenure is examined.

Several limitations bound these conclusions. Because valid instruments for farmland ownership are difficult to identify, we rely on matching to improve comparability rather than to establish causality; the design reduces selection on observables and does not address selection on unobservables, so the estimates are best read as conditional associations. Tenure is self-reported and, in a setting where customary and statutory conceptions of ownership do not coincide, is a contested category rather than a merely mismeasured one. The tenure detail is also unevenly available across rounds, so the disaggregated contrasts rest on narrower foundations than the aggregate comparison. Finally, the aggregate ownership gap is small enough that, as the robustness analysis shows, its magnitude and sign cannot be separated from the assumed distribution of the inefficiency term.

Within those bounds, several policy implications follow. First, efforts to raise agricultural productivity are unlikely to succeed through land redistribution or documentation alone, since neither margin delivers a measurable performance premium in these data; complementary support systems that reduce the risks of insecure tenure are the more promising lever. Second, programmes aimed at boosting technology adoption, such as input subsidies, mechanisation services, and extension support, should reach farmers operating without ownership, who face structural barriers to improving productivity but are not less efficient users of the technology they can access. Third, the heterogeneity documented across regions and crops suggests that tailored policies addressing specific land-use contexts and cropping systems are more likely to succeed than blanket reforms.

Future research should pursue the causal mechanisms these data cannot isolate, using panel or experimental designs capable of separating tenure from the conditions that accompany it, and should examine how access to finance, infrastructure, and market linkages interact with tenure to shape productivity. The reversal documented here, in which documentation and transfer rights track lower rather than higher meta-frontier efficiency, is not explained by this design and merits direct investigation.

Despite these limitations, the findings point to the value of land policy and agricultural investment strategies that treat secure tenure as one input among several rather than as a sufficient condition for productivity growth. Addressing these disparities matters not only for productivity but also for inclusive rural development and economic resilience. By creating an enabling environment for all farmers, regardless of landholding status, Ghana can move closer to an agricultural transformation whose gains are broadly shared.
